She started her GLP-1 medication at 47. Within six weeks, the woman who danced in our kitchen every Sunday morning stopped coming out of the bathroom.

I'm not exaggerating.

Rachel had fought her weight since our youngest was born. Twelve years of calorie counting. Weight Watchers. Keto. Slimming World. A gym membership she used five days a week for eight months straight.

Nothing worked. Not long enough.

When her GP started her on a GLP-1 medication, it felt like a miracle. The food noise went quiet. The scales moved. She was happy for the first time in years.

Then the constipation started.

At first it was two or three days. She'd mention it casually. "Probably just adjusting."

Then it was five days. She bought Movicol.

Then a week. She added fibre gummies, stool softeners, prune juice.

Then it was ten days.

I found her on the bathroom floor at 11pm on a Tuesday, knees pulled to her chest, tears running down her face.

"I can't do this," she whispered. "It feels like cement inside me. Nothing will move."

That was the moment I stopped trusting what we had been told.

The GP Who Didn't Listen

I went with her to her next appointment.

Dr Sheehan had been her GP for nine years. Good doctor. Thorough. But when Rachel described what was happening, his response made my blood pressure spike.

"Constipation is a common side effect of GLP-1 medications," he said, typing on his laptop. "Are you drinking enough water?"

"She drinks around 2.3 litres a day," I said.

"Fibre?"

"She's taking fibre gummies and Fybogel. They're making her MORE bloated."

He nodded. "Some patients find that fibre can bulk up in a slowed digestive system. Try cutting it back. Add some movement. Walking after meals."

Rachel stared at him. "I walk three miles every morning."

"Give it time," he said. "Most patients adjust."

"It's been two months," I said.

He looked at me with that practised patience doctors use when a partner gets involved.

"The medication is working. She's lost a stone. We need to stay the course." He scribbled on his notepad. "If it gets severe, we can try a prescription laxative. But I'd rather not add another medication."

We left with nothing.

Rachel was quiet the whole drive home.

"He didn't even examine me," she said, staring out the window.

I gripped the steering wheel and didn't answer.

Because she was right.

What I Found at 2am

That night I couldn't sleep.

I sat in the living room with my laptop and started searching. Not the forums. Not the Facebook groups where everyone tells you to drink more water and eat more fibre. I wanted to understand what was actually happening inside her body.

I searched: "why does GLP-1 cause constipation" and "why fibre makes GLP-1 constipation worse."

Most results were the usual advice. Drink more water. Add fibre. Exercise. Everything she was already doing.

Then I found a video from a gastroenterologist who explained something nobody had mentioned.

It wasn't about fibre. It wasn't about water intake.

It was about fuel.

He said your colon doesn't just move on its own. It needs fuel. Specific molecules called short-chain fatty acids, or SCFAs.

He compared it to a car engine.

Your colon runs on SCFAs the way a car runs on petrol. Normally, the bacteria in your gut produce this fuel all day long by fermenting fibre in your colon. That fuel tells your colon to contract and push things through. It feeds the cells that line your colon wall. Without it, your colon sits idle. Like a car with an empty petrol tank.

I paused the video. Stared at the screen.

Then he explained the part that made me want to throw my laptop:

GLP-1 medications slow everything down. That's the point. Slower digestion means you feel full longer, eat less, lose weight.

But the slowdown doesn't just affect your stomach.

It reaches your colon.

When transit slows, the bacteria in your gut get less material to ferment. Less fermentation means less SCFA production. Less fuel for your colon.

And then it spirals.

Slower colon means even less fermentation. Even less fermentation means even less fuel. Even less fuel means an even slower colon. Every day the cycle tightens.

That's why Rachel's constipation was getting WORSE over time. Not better. The cycle couldn't break itself because the medication kept the initial slowdown in place.

I sat there in the dark and felt my chest tighten.

Because suddenly every failed remedy made sense:

Fibre doesn't fix this. Fibre is raw material for the bacteria to ferment. But in a gut that's barely moving, fibre just SITS there. It piles up. It bloats. The factory is shut down. Dumping more raw materials at the door doesn't restart the factory.

Probiotics don't fix this. Probiotics add more bacteria. But those bacteria need to ferment fibre to produce SCFAs. In a slowed gut, they can't do their job. You're hiring workers for a factory with no power.

Laxatives don't fix this. Laxatives force ONE bowel movement by overriding the system. They don't restore fuel production. They push the car downhill once. The tank is still empty tomorrow.

Every single thing Rachel had tried was targeting the wrong problem.

I looked at the bedroom door. She was in there, probably awake, probably bloated, probably wondering if she'd have to quit the medication that finally silenced the food noise.

And I thought: somebody has to be delivering this fuel directly instead of hoping the gut will produce it.

Because that's what she needed. Not more bacteria. Not more fibre. Not more chemical laxatives.

She needed the fuel itself.

The Research That Changed Everything

I kept reading.

I found a clinical study showing that the primary organic acid in fermented kombucha culture is acetic acid. Acetic acid IS acetate. One of the three main SCFAs your colon uses as fuel.

Kombucha doesn't wait for bacteria to ferment fibre into SCFAs. It delivers the fuel molecule directly.

Like pouring petrol into an empty tank instead of waiting for the petrol station to reopen.

Then I found another study. Controlled trial. People consuming kombucha showed improved stool consistency and reduced incomplete bowel evacuation.

A third study showed that specific probiotic strains, L. plantarum and B. coagulans, could survive stomach acid and actually improve motility in constipated adults. B. coagulans reduced indigestion by 65% compared to placebo in a randomised trial.

And then the piece that connected it all:

Dandelion root contains 40% inulin by dry weight. Inulin is a prebiotic that specifically feeds butyrate-producing bacteria. Butyrate provides 70 to 80% of the energy your colon cells need to function.

Slippery elm produces SCFAs during its own breakdown AND coats the gut lining with a protective mucilage.

I sat back and stared at the screen.

The immediate problem: her colon was starving for fuel. Kombucha delivers that fuel directly.

The long-term problem: her gut bacteria couldn't produce their own fuel. Prebiotics and targeted probiotics rebuild that production line.

Both problems. One approach. Fuel delivery now. Factory rebuild over time.

I woke Rachel up.

"I found something," I said.

She looked at me with that tired, hollowed-out expression I'd been seeing for weeks.

"Nate," she said. "Please. I can't handle another thing that doesn't work."

"This is different. Everything you've tried was targeting the wrong problem. Your colon is starving for a specific fuel. And there's one thing that delivers it directly."

She didn't say anything for a long time.

Then: "What do we have to lose?"

What Happened When She Tried It

The next morning I started researching.

I needed something that combined kombucha culture with prebiotics and the right probiotic strains. Not just a basic probiotic capsule. Not just kombucha in a bottle.

Most gut supplements for people on GLP-1 medications are rubbish.

Standard probiotics use strains that die in the stomach, especially with the delayed emptying from a GLP-1. The bacteria sit in acid for hours and never reach the colon alive.

Fibre supplements dump more bulk into an already stalled system.

Cheap kombucha drinks are mostly sugar water with trace amounts of culture.

I found one company that combined the right things:

Kombucha powder delivering direct SCFAs. L. plantarum and B. coagulans, both proven to survive stomach acid and improve motility. Dandelion root and slippery elm for prebiotic support and gut lining protection.

It was called Glissé. Organic-certified. Third-party tested. They published their Certificate of Analysis right on the site.

I almost scrolled past it. The website didn't look like the big supplement brands.

But the formulation matched exactly what the research said her colon needed.

I ordered a bottle.

I didn't tell Rachel. I didn't want to get her hopes up again.

When it arrived three days later, I waited until evening.

She was sitting on the sofa, hot water bottle on her stomach, looking miserable. She'd skipped dinner because eating made the bloating worse.

"Try these," I said, handing her the bottle.

She looked at me. Then at the bottle.

"What is it?"

"Kombucha gummies. With prebiotics and probiotics designed for people on GLP-1 medications."

That tired, sceptical look. The one that said: We've been through this before.

"Two gummies," I said. "That's it. If nothing happens in two weeks, we stop."

She took two gummies. Chewed them. Made a face that said "not bad." Went back to her hot water bottle.

I didn't expect much that night.

Week One: "Something Feels Different"

The first three days, nothing.

Day four, Rachel said something at breakfast that made me look up from my coffee.

"I feel less... stuck."

"What do you mean?"

"I don't know. Like things are moving. A little."

Day five, she had a bowel movement. Not dramatic. Not the explosive Movicol-driven kind that left her cramping for hours. Just... normal. Quiet.

She came out of the bathroom and looked at me.

"That's the first time in three weeks it didn't hurt," she said.

I didn't say anything. Too early. Could be coincidence.

Day six. Another one. No straining. No pain.

Day seven. Same.

I was paying attention now.

Week Two: "I Forgot About My Stomach"

By the end of the second week, the change was undeniable.

Rachel was eating dinner with me again. Full portions. No hot water bottle afterwards.

The bloating that had made her look six months pregnant since starting the medication was visibly reduced. She put on a pair of jeans she hadn't worn in two months.

"They fit," she said, sounding confused. "They actually fit."

But the thing that got me was what she said Thursday evening.

We were watching TV. She turned to me.

"I forgot about my stomach today."

"What?"

"I went through the whole day and didn't think about my stomach once. I didn't plan my meals around whether I'd bloat. I didn't avoid eating because I was scared of the pain. I just... ate. And was fine."

She paused.

"I can't remember the last time that happened."

Week Four: "I Feel Like Myself Again"

A month in, Rachel woke me up early on a Saturday.

"Let's go to the farmers' market," she said. "I want to walk around. I want to eat something from one of the stands and not worry about it."

We hadn't done that in four months.

We spent the whole morning together. She tried a peach from a vendor and laughed when the juice ran down her chin. She bought herbs for a recipe she'd been too sick to make.

Walking home, she looped her arm through mine.

"I feel like myself again," she said.

Then, quieter: "I didn't realise how bad it had gotten until it stopped."

I didn't say anything. I just held her arm tighter.

Week Six: Dr Sheehan's Appointment

Rachel had a routine follow-up with Dr Sheehan.

I went with her.

When the nurse asked about her medications, Rachel mentioned the Glissé gummies.

Dr Sheehan pulled up her chart. "How are the digestive symptoms?"

"Gone," Rachel said. "Daily bowel movements. No bloating. No pain."

He looked up from his screen. "Gone?"

"I've been taking a fermented kombucha supplement with prebiotics. My husband found research about how GLP-1 medications can starve the colon of the fuel it needs to move."

Dr Sheehan looked at his notes. Then back at Rachel.

"Well," he said. "Your weight loss is continuing. You're tolerating the medication. And the constipation has resolved."

Pause.

"I'm not familiar with that particular connection. But your results speak for themselves. Continue what you're doing."

That was the best we were going to get. And honestly? It was enough.

Why Most Gut Supplements for GLP-1 Users Don't Work

After Rachel's results, I told three women at her gym who were dealing with the same thing.

Two of them tried generic probiotics from Amazon.

Nothing changed.

I wasn't surprised. Because I'd already learned this the hard way:

Most probiotics do NOT work for people on GLP-1 medications. The delayed stomach emptying means bacteria sit in acid for hours. Most strains die before reaching the colon. You're swallowing dead bacteria.

And even the ones that survive? They need to ferment fibre to produce SCFAs. In a slowed gut, that fermentation barely happens. The workers show up but the factory has no power.

Glissé was the only supplement I found that delivers SCFAs directly through kombucha culture AND includes spore-forming probiotics that actually survive GLP-1 stomach conditions AND has the prebiotics to rebuild the gut's own fuel production over time.

That's why it works. And that's why the cheap alternatives don't.

If Your Wife, Partner, or Someone You Love Is on a GLP-1 Medication, Please Read This

Ask yourself:

If you said yes to even one of those, it's not "just adjusting."

My father took Movicol every morning for twelve years. He died at 64 of complications from chronic constipation.

Three months ago I sat in the same consulting-room chair he sat in and my GP reached for the same prescription.

I almost said yes — until my husband asked one question that would have saved my father's life.

I'm 44.

My father has been gone for nine years now. The spring our youngest started Reception.

The death certificate said "complications from chronic constipation, sepsis pathway." I didn't even understand what that meant until I read the discharge summary on the plane home from the funeral.

He was a quiet man. A bridge engineer for the council highways department for thirty-six years. He measured things for a living.

The Movicol showed up on his kitchen counter the year I turned 30.

His GP said the line I've thought about every week since.

"This is your new best friend now."

That exact phrase.

My father wrote it down on a Post-it inside the kitchen cabinet. I found it cleaning out the house. New best friend. In his engineer's handwriting.

For twelve years he scooped the white powder into his orange juice every morning at 6:15am. I watched him do it from my teenage kitchen, and then later from the kitchen I came home to visit.

He'd say "I'm regular as a clock."

He'd say it like a small joke at family dinners. Like a man reporting from a bridge inspection.

I believed him.

The year before he died, he started saying his belly felt "tight." He was 63. The GP said keep up the Movicol, maybe try a little Fybogel with it.

He did.

The week he died I didn't know how bad it had gotten. The hospital said sepsis. The hospital said impaction. The hospital used the word "perforation" and I asked them to please not use the word "perforation" with my mother in the room.

Twelve years of managed output.

He died of the thing they were managing.

I started slipping around the time my fortieth birthday came and went.

Every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth.

By 42 it was every four to five days at best.

The bloat showed up at 8pm like a guest who would not leave. I stopped wearing my wrap dress because I look six months pregnant by dinner. Stopped tucking shirts in. Started pulling jumpers around my waist in every photo.

I dread thinking about when I will poo.

I stopped saying that out loud somewhere around my 40th birthday because I could hear my mother saying it about my father.

The strain hour at 6am, the door locked, my knees pulled up to my chest, my eyes closed for ninety minutes while the rest of the house slept.

Pebble stools when I did go. Rabbit pellets. Blood on the paper one morning — I cried in the bathroom and then I went to work.

The drawer.

I stood in front of it one night and I made myself list it out loud.

Movicol. White powder, the orange juice in the morning.

Fybogel. Three orange tubs stacked in the back.

Magnesium citrate. The green-and-yellow bottle I'd chug on Sunday nights. Tastes like grapefruit lighter fluid.

Magnesium glycinate. The calmer one. Didn't really move anything.

Senna. The brown tablets. The whip I'd take when I had a flight Tuesday.

Dulcolax suppositories. The box in the back. The emergency drawer.

Milk of Magnesia. Four months of chalky nightly chugs. Bloated belly that wouldn't quit. Stopped working after three rounds.

Castor oil. Three days. The smell. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Never again.

Probiotics. We fell for Optibac. £30 a month for six months. Three good weeks. Then nothing.

Senna tea. The kettle on at 9pm every Sunday.

Prune juice. Every morning until I gagged at the sight of the bottle.

Triphala. Two weeks of working, then nothing.

Fibre gummies. Two different brands. Made the bloat worse.

The toilet stool under the bathroom sink.

The colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.

A pelvic-floor physio referral I cancelled twice and never went to.

I closed the drawer.

Stood there in the dark.

Half of those were in my father's cabinet too. I'd been buying them my whole life and not seeing it.

This past New Year I drove down to help my mother sort my father's old papers.

We sat at the same kitchen table I grew up at.

In the back of the cabinet behind the coffee mugs, I found an unopened Movicol packet.

I held it.

Sat down with it in my hand.

Set it on the counter next to my coffee.

Drove home that night.

Booked the first available appointment with my new GP — my old one had retired the year before — and made a note in my phone to actually go this time.

Three weeks later I was sitting in Consulting Room 4 of the same medical centre my father had used for fifteen years.

I didn't realise that until I walked in and saw the framed lithograph of a covered bridge on the wall.

Same lithograph my father used to make fun of. A bridge engineer making fun of a bridge lithograph for fifteen years.

The chair.

The vinyl consulting chair with the cracked armrest.

The same chair.

I sat down in it and I could feel my father sitting in it.

My husband came with me because I had been crying in the car for two weeks. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.

The GP was kind. He was thorough. He listened for six minutes.

Then he said "you've tried a lot."

Pulled out the prescription pad.

"Let's start you on daily Movicol. It'll be your new best friend."

The exact phrase.

Twelve years late.

I almost said yes. My hand was already reaching for the script.

My husband leaned forward in the side chair.

Quiet. Not aggressive. The way he asks the mechanic things.

"Before she takes that to the chemist — can someone look at what's actually broken? Her dad was on this for twelve years."

The GP paused.

Said he could refer me to a functional-medicine specialist if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card out of his desk drawer and handed it to me.

Dr Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. Cottage office on Maple Street.

I took the card.

Walked out without the prescription.

Sat in the car park for forty minutes before I could start the car.

I almost cancelled the appointment with Dr Aurelia twice.

Two hundred pounds for an intake form that asks me about my father felt like grief tourism.

I drove there anyway.

A converted cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. The smell of bergamot tea coming out of what used to be a dining room.

The receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.

Dr Aurelia came out herself to call my name. Not a healthcare assistant. Mid-fifties, grey bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain.

She booked one patient per hour. I was the one patient.

The intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.

She didn't talk about treatment that first visit. She said: "Before we change anything, I want to see what's actually there."

Ordered a microbiome stool panel.

Three hundred and forty pounds privately.

I almost didn't send it in.

I sent it in.

Ten days later the results came back and we booked a follow-up.

Second appointment.

I sat on my bathroom floor at 1 a.m. with a latex glove on my hand, reading a stranger’s step-by-step instructions on Reddit for how to dig a faecal impaction out of yourself.

I’d been to two NHS urgent treatment centres in ten days. Both told me the same thing: try Movicol and Fybogel.

I’d already tried Movicol and Fybogel.

I’d already tried multiple enemas. I’d been feeling the same piece trying to come out for three weeks, and every time I finally went, it was still there.

And that’s how a grown woman ends up scrolling through a subreddit for a how-to at one in the morning.

I’m 38. I need to back up a little, because if you’re reading this on a bathroom floor of your own, some of this is going to sound familiar and some of it is going to sound insane, and I want you to know which is which.

Three months ago my partner got a job at the other end of the country and we moved. New city. New flat. New bathroom that still didn’t feel like home.

Old constipation.

I’d had it for about four years. Slow slide. Going every day, then every other day, then twice a week, then a bad week here, a bad week there. It started after a course of antibiotics for a sinus infection a few years back, and it never came all the way back.

For a long time I managed it the way you manage a dripping tap. Movicol every morning with my coffee, religiously. If that stopped working, I’d add Fybogel. If Fybogel failed, I’d take magnesium citrate before bed.

It wasn’t great. It was fine.

Then six months ago the Movicol started going wrong.

What came out went sticky and shiny — the same way an old floor gets when it’s been mopped with the wrong thing. I could tell my body was doing something with the powder it hadn’t been doing before, and it wasn’t a good something. I Googled it once, saw a Reddit thread of women describing the same shiny mass, and closed the tab.

I added the Fybogel.

Two days without a bowel movement. Bloated up like a balloon.

I stopped the Fybogel and added magnesium citrate at night. It worked for maybe three weeks, then I started needing more of it. Then I started waking up with the kind of brain fog and low-level sadness I could not afford at work.

Then the move.

Three weeks after we arrived, I realised I hadn’t properly gone in five days.

Then a week.

Then I sat on the toilet for an hour one Sunday morning and got what my body would only describe as a handful of rabbit pellets. I could still feel a mass sitting inside me.

Higher up.

Not going anywhere.

That was the beginning of the three weeks.

Every day I’d go a little. Every day the same piece would still be there afterwards, trying to come out and not coming out.

“When will I poo?”

That is the exact sentence I typed into my Notes app one night and did not delete.

I dreaded every meal. I dreaded pouring my coffee. I dreaded the syringe I had started keeping in the bathroom drawer to flush out whatever I could still feel after every failed attempt.

I know how that sounds.

I know because I typed it into a search bar once and immediately deleted my history, the way you delete something you do not want your partner to see.

I went to an NHS urgent treatment centre.

The doctor was in his early thirties and had been on shift for eight hours. He asked what I’d tried.

“Movicol, Fybogel, magnesium citrate, senna tea, Milk of Magnesia.”

“Well, try Movicol and Fybogel.”

“I already have.”

“Sometimes it takes time.”

Ten days later, I went to another urgent treatment centre.

Different building. Different doctor. Same advice.

“Pick up some Movicol and Fybogel. You’ll feel better in a few days.”

I sat in the car park for fifteen minutes, staring at my steering wheel.

At home, I had a laxative drawer that looked like the aisle he’d sent me to. I could not understand why they thought Movicol and Fybogel would work when three enemas from the chemist hadn’t.

That was a Tuesday.

I bought the third enema in ten days.

A bottle of magnesium citrate. The bright orange one that tastes like a cough sweet’s evil twin.

A box of suppositories I had absolutely no plan for.

And a packet of chewing gum, so the whole basket wasn’t laxatives.

When I got home, my partner asked how it went.

“Fine.”

He did not ask anything else because I’d already trained him not to.

The words “faecal impaction” had not left my mouth in three weeks.

Not to him. Not to anyone.

I did not know how to open that door.

At ten o’clock that night, I used the enema.

I sat on the bathroom floor for an hour with my back against the bath. Almost nothing came out except more rabbit pellets.

The piece I could feel was still there.

I did not cry.

I sat on the tiles with the empty bottle beside me and stared at the grout.

Then I picked up my phone.

I do not remember what I typed first. Something about faecal impaction. Something with the words “how do I know if”.

Then something less careful.

The subreddit came up.

r/Constipation.

The manual disimpaction thread was the third result.

I opened it.

The top comment was from a woman explaining how she’d learnt to work the stool out from outside her body when a contraction came. She used the word “toothpaste” the way someone might use it in a cookery blog.

She was kind. Matter-of-fact. She was writing to help.

I did not want to be the woman she was writing to help.

I read it three more times.

Underneath was a comment from a man on methadone who kept a small tub of Vaseline and a box of gloves in his bathroom cupboard.

Below his was someone who used a condom over her middle finger and had done it, in her own words, about twenty-five times.

I closed the app.

Then I opened it again.

At around 12.30 a.m., I walked into the kitchen. Beneath the sink was the plastic box where I kept the yellow gloves I used to clean the bath.

I took one out.

Walked back to the bathroom.

Sat down on the tiles.

Put the glove on and pulled it over my wrist the way I’d once seen a nurse do it.

Then I sat there with the glove on.

I was 38 years old. I had a university degree, a partner who loved me, savings, a job and a mobile contract.

And I was about to reach inside myself on my own bathroom floor because two men in polo shirts had told me twice that I should really try more fibre.

I did not do it.

I do not know how to explain what stopped me.

It was not willpower. It was not exactly shame.

In the split second before I moved, I decided to scroll one more time. Find one more comment. Make sure this was really the answer.

I scrolled.

The next comment was long. Longer than the others.

The username included “hospice_rn” and a number I took to mean her years at the bedside.

Eighteen.

She was not replying to the original poster. She was replying to the top comment.

I read what she had written.

Then I read it again.

Then I took a screenshot because I did not trust myself to hold on to anything in that moment.

I am going to type it out the way I have reread it since.

I have reread it a lot.

“Please do not put your fingers up there. Not because you’re disgusting for considering it — you’re desperate, and nobody at either of those urgent treatment centres did their job. But there’s a reason none of that has worked for you, and it isn’t your fibre.”

“I’ve been a hospice nurse for eighteen years. I’ve seen a lot of impactions. Nobody’s colon ever needed the fingers. Some of them needed something to fire the contraction that had gone silent. Different thing.”

“Here’s what nobody explains to you at an urgent treatment centre.”

“You’ve been treating the stool. Softening it. Bulking it. Forcing it.”

“But the stool was never the actual problem.”

“Your colon is supposed to contract once or twice a day and clear itself out. That contraction is what you feel as the urge.”

“And that contraction is what hasn’t been firing for you.”

“Deep inside your colon wall are cells that fire it. They’re called pacemaker cells — the same idea as the ones that keep your heart beating in rhythm.”

“In some people, years of processed food, stress or a rough course of antibiotics allow free radicals inside the colon wall to damage those cells.”

“The contraction weakens. The urge fades. The stool sits.”

“And it does not show up on any scan.”

“It’s happening at a cellular level. No X-ray, colonoscopy or urgent-treatment-centre doctor with a ten-minute appointment is going to see it.”

“That’s why the answer is always more fibre and water. The tests come back normal, so they assume you are.”

“Slice an apple and leave it on the worktop. Within twenty minutes, it browns.”

“That’s oxidation — free radicals breaking down the flesh. The same chemistry that causes metal to rust.”

“Now squeeze lemon juice over a fresh slice. It stays white.”

“That’s an antioxidant stopping the damage.”

“Kombucha is a potent antioxidant. For those cells, it’s the lemon juice.”

“Before you buy a crate of kombucha from the health-food shop — don’t. That’s the wrong form.”

“Heat strips away the antioxidants, and shelf-stable bottles have been heated. You’d have to drink several a day, along with all that sugar, and still wouldn’t get close.”

“What you want is concentrated kombucha extract. Standardised. In a form that survives your stomach.”

“I keep a pouch of Glissé on my worktop. One gummy a day.”

“It contains a concentrated kombucha acid complex, two probiotic strains with trials for chronic constipation, slippery elm for the gut lining and dandelion root to feed the strains.”

“All in a berry gummy that passes the morning-coffee test.”

“There’s a money-back guarantee, so if it does nothing for you, send it back.”

“It will not clear whatever is sitting inside you tonight. Nothing on this list will.”

“That is what the urgent treatment centres should have told you.”

“But it is the only thing I’ve seen bring the urge back naturally for the patients I’ve looked after.”

“You’re not broken.”

“Your colon hasn’t forgotten how to do this.”

“The cells that fire the contraction have been oxidising, the way that apple browns.”

“Address that.”

“Don’t dig.”

That was her comment.

I read it three more times.

I sat on the tiles with the glove still on my hand and stared at my phone.

Some of what she said I understood immediately, the way you understand a punchline after the setup has dragged on for an hour. Some of it I understood like a foreign language I knew only a hundred words of.

But it did the one thing I could not do for myself.

It gave me a reason.

Not a fix. A reason.

For twenty-one days, I had been living inside a body I could not explain to a doctor. And a stranger with eighteen years of hospice experience had, in a Reddit thread I was ashamed to be reading, given me a plain answer for why fibre and Movicol were not touching this.

The cells meant to fire the contraction were oxidising. The scans were looking for blockages and disease and coming back clear because they were looking in the wrong place.

I took off the glove and set it on the tiles.

Then I opened a new tab and typed “Glissé”.

The website loaded.

A cream, green and pink pouch with a red raspberry on the side. Everything the nurse had described was there: concentrated kombucha extract, two probiotic strains, slippery elm, dandelion root and a 90-day money-back guarantee.

I read the page twice.

I had been burnt before. I fell for Seed’s advertising once and never fully got that money back in emotional terms. I did not want to spend £60 because of a decision made on a bathroom floor.

I bought one pouch.

Not the two-pack. Not the subscription. The single pouch. £25, plus delivery.

If it did nothing, I would send it back.

I put my phone face down, threw the glove into the bin beneath the sink and washed my hands with hot water for longer than I needed to.

I got into bed at 1.47 a.m.

My partner rolled over.

“Where were you?”

“The bathroom.”

“You all right?”

“Yeah.”

“Come here.”

I did.

I want to be honest about what happened next, because if you are reading this from somewhere close to the bathroom floor I was on, the last thing you need is a fake miracle timeline.

Week one, nothing changed.

I took one gummy every morning with my coffee. I still used an enema on day three. I still used the syringe in the bathroom drawer to flush out the last of what I could feel.

I did not expect anything. I had stopped expecting anything a long time ago.

Week two, on a Wednesday, I went on my own.

No enema. No syringe.

It was not much, but it was not rabbit pellets. It was one soft, whole, ordinary bowel movement at 7.15 in the morning, with the door not quite closed because I had not planned for it.

I sat there afterwards and did not know what to do with my hands.

I told nobody. I was not sure it counted.

Two days later, it happened again.

Week three, the urge started returning on its own.

Not every morning. Two days out of seven, then three.

The signal.

The thing I had not felt in almost a year.

It arrives more quietly than you remember. Like a tap on a door instead of a doorbell.

I stopped using the syringe.

In week four, I put it in the drawer with all the failed things and closed it.

By week five, I was going most mornings.

No Movicol. No magnesium.

During the worst week, I had booked another NHS urgent treatment centre appointment because I did not know what else to do.

I rang and cancelled it.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

I did not mention the Reddit thread.

In week seven, I stood in front of the bathroom mirror at 10 p.m. and realised my lower belly was flat.

Not held-in flat.

Just — flat.

The way it used to be.

I had not thought about it in three months. It had come back without asking me first.

I did not cry.

I looked at it for a minute, then switched off the light.

I have not opened the drawer beneath the sink in a month.

I ordered again last week — the two-pack this time. It arrived on Thursday. I put it beside the kettle.

There is one part I have not told you because it is the hardest.

I never told my partner about the glove.

After week five, I told him I had been badly constipated. He knew that. I told him it had become bad enough for two NHS urgent treatment centres. He knew that too because he had driven me to the second one.

But I did not tell him about the manual disimpaction thread.

I did not tell him about the yellow cleaning glove, the box beneath the sink or the 1 a.m. searches I deleted three times.

I hope I will eventually.

He is a good man. He would not have flinched.

But I want you to understand what I was minutes away from doing, alone on a tiled floor in a city I had lived in for three months, because two doctors in two different buildings had given me the same advice and neither had asked why it was not working.

If the drawer beneath your sink looks like mine did —

if your Google history contains “how do I know if I’m impacted?” —

if your tests keep coming back normal while you keep getting worse —

it is not your fibre.

It is happening at a cellular level, and no urgent treatment centre is going to look for it.

The cells that fire the contraction have been oxidising quietly for years, while everything in your drawer treats the stool that a working contraction was supposed to move.

Address the cells.

Concentrated kombucha extract with the antioxidants intact. Standardised. One gummy a day.

Slippery elm, dandelion root and two probiotic strains with trials in people with chronic constipation.

All in one small berry gummy from a Glissé pouch beside the kettle.

A 90-day money-back guarantee.

If it does nothing for you within three months, send it back.

I nearly put my hand where a scalpel belongs because two doctors told me my body was fine.

It was not fine.

It was just quiet.

I bought the third enema in ten days.

A bottle of magnesium citrate. The bright orange one that tastes like a cough sweet’s evil twin.

A box of suppositories I had absolutely no plan for.

And a packet of chewing gum, so the whole basket wasn’t laxatives.

“Fine.”

He did not ask anything else because I’d already trained him not to.

The words “faecal impaction” had not left my mouth in three weeks.

Not to him. Not to anyone.

I did not know how to open that door.

The piece I could feel was still there.

I did not cry.

I sat on the tiles with the empty bottle beside me and stared at the grout.

I do not remember what I typed first. Something about faecal impaction. Something with the words “how do I know if”.

The subreddit came up.

r/Constipation.

Below his was someone who used a condom over her middle finger and had done it, in her own words, about twenty-five times.

I closed the app.

I took one out.

Walked back to the bathroom.

Sat down on the tiles.

Put the glove on and pulled it over my wrist the way I’d once seen a nurse do it.

I did not do it.

It was not willpower. It was not exactly shame.

I scrolled.

The next comment was long. Longer than the others.

The username included “hospice_rn” and a number I took to mean her years at the bedside.

Eighteen.

She was not replying to the original poster. She was replying to the top comment.

I read what she had written.

Then I read it again.

Then I took a screenshot because I did not trust myself to hold on to anything in that moment.

I am going to type it out the way I have reread it since.

“Please do not put your fingers up there. Not because you’re disgusting for considering it — you’re desperate, and nobody at either of those urgent treatment centres did their job. But there’s a reason none of that has worked for you, and it isn’t your fibre.”

“I’ve been a hospice nurse for eighteen years. I’ve seen a lot of impactions. Nobody’s colon ever needed the fingers. Some of them needed something to fire the contraction that had gone silent. Different thing.”

“Here’s what nobody explains to you at an urgent treatment centre.”

“You’ve been treating the stool. Softening it. Bulking it. Forcing it.”

“But the stool was never the actual problem.”

“Your colon is supposed to contract once or twice a day and clear itself out. That contraction is what you feel as the urge.”

“And that contraction is what hasn’t been firing for you.”

“Deep inside your colon wall are cells that fire it. They’re called pacemaker cells — the same idea as the ones that keep your heart beating in rhythm.”

“In some people, years of processed food, stress or a rough course of antibiotics allow free radicals inside the colon wall to damage those cells.”

“The contraction weakens. The urge fades. The stool sits.”

“And it does not show up on any scan.”

“It’s happening at a cellular level. No X-ray, colonoscopy or urgent-treatment-centre doctor with a ten-minute appointment is going to see it.”

“That’s why the answer is always more fibre and water. The tests come back normal, so they assume you are.”

“What you want is concentrated kombucha extract. Standardised. In a form that survives your stomach.”

“It contains a concentrated kombucha acid complex, two probiotic strains with trials for chronic constipation, slippery elm for the gut lining and dandelion root to feed the strains.”

“All in a berry gummy that passes the morning-coffee test.”

“There’s a money-back guarantee, so if it does nothing for you, send it back.”

“It will not clear whatever is sitting inside you tonight. Nothing on this list will.”

“That is what the urgent treatment centres should have told you.”

“But it is the only thing I’ve seen bring the urge back naturally for the patients I’ve looked after.”

“You’re not broken.”

“Your colon hasn’t forgotten how to do this.”

“The cells that fire the contraction have been oxidising, the way that apple browns.”

“Address that.”

“Don’t dig.”

That was her comment.

I read it three more times.

But it did the one thing I could not do for myself.

It gave me a reason.

Not a fix. A reason.

For twenty-one days, I had been living inside a body I could not explain to a doctor. And a stranger with eighteen years of hospice experience had, in a Reddit thread I was ashamed to be reading, given me a plain answer for why fibre and Movicol were not touching this.

The cells meant to fire the contraction were oxidising. The scans were looking for blockages and disease and coming back clear because they were looking in the wrong place.

The website loaded.

I read the page twice.

Not the two-pack. Not the subscription. The single pouch. £25, plus delivery.

My partner rolled over.

“Where were you?”

“The bathroom.”

“You all right?”

“Yeah.”

“Come here.”

I did not expect anything. I had stopped expecting anything a long time ago.

No enema. No syringe.

It was not much, but it was not rabbit pellets. It was one soft, whole, ordinary bowel movement at 7.15 in the morning, with the door not quite closed because I had not planned for it.

I sat there afterwards and did not know what to do with my hands.

I told nobody. I was not sure it counted.

Two days later, it happened again.

Week three, the urge started returning on its own.

Not every morning. Two days out of seven, then three.

The signal.

The thing I had not felt in almost a year.

It arrives more quietly than you remember. Like a tap on a door instead of a doorbell.

I stopped using the syringe.

In week four, I put it in the drawer with all the failed things and closed it.

By week five, I was going most mornings.

No Movicol. No magnesium.

During the worst week, I had booked another NHS urgent treatment centre appointment because I did not know what else to do.

I rang and cancelled it.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

I did not mention the Reddit thread.

In week seven, I stood in front of the bathroom mirror at 10 p.m. and realised my lower belly was flat.

Not held-in flat.

Just — flat.

The way it used to be.

I had not thought about it in three months. It had come back without asking me first.

I did not cry.

I looked at it for a minute, then switched off the light.

I have not opened the drawer beneath the sink in a month.

I ordered again last week — the two-pack this time. It arrived on Thursday. I put it beside the kettle.

I never told my partner about the glove.

I did not tell him about the yellow cleaning glove, the box beneath the sink or the 1 a.m. searches I deleted three times.

If the drawer beneath your sink looks like mine did —

if your Google history contains “how do I know if I’m impacted?” —

if your tests keep coming back normal while you keep getting worse —

it is not your fibre.

It is happening at a cellular level, and no urgent treatment centre is going to look for it.

The cells that fire the contraction have been oxidising quietly for years, while everything in your drawer treats the stool that a working contraction was supposed to move.

Address the cells.

Slippery elm, dandelion root and two probiotic strains with trials in people with chronic constipation.

All in one small berry gummy from a Glissé pouch beside the kettle.

A 90-day money-back guarantee.

If it does nothing for you within three months, send it back.

It was not fine.

It was just quiet.

I've been a consultant colorectal surgeon for twelve years. 

And if you go days without opening your bowels, strain until you sweat, and your GP keeps brushing you off with “more fibre, more water”... I'm about to tell you the one thing no one who trained me ever had a reason to teach me — and why I performed seventy-one operations before I understood it.

By the end of this, you're going to be furious. I know I was. I'm still furious with myself.

My name is Miss Ellen Walsh. Consultant colorectal surgeon on the GMC Specialist Register. Twelve years operating on the lower bowel. Advanced fellowship training at one of the busiest colorectal units in the UK. Seventy-one colectomies.

And I'm breaking ranks with my own profession to tell you this.

There are three things you need to understand.

One — your body is screaming that something is wrong, and it's right.

Two — there is a real, specific cause.

And three — there is a reason you've never heard its name from a doctor. Not a conspiracy. Something more ordinary: you can't patent it, so nobody who trained us ever had a reason to put it on the board.

I'll prove that with my own career.

Let me tell you about one of my patients.

Her name was Denise. Fifty-one years old.

For six straight years, she had lived like this.

By every evening, her stomach was so swollen she looked six months pregnant. She couldn't fasten the jeans she'd worn for a decade. She'd been regular her whole life, and suddenly she had the gut of a stranger.

By the end of most weeks, she hadn't had a proper bowel movement in eleven days. When something finally moved, she strained so hard her haemorrhoids bled.

She stopped accepting dinner invitations. Stopped travelling. Started avoiding anywhere she didn't already know where the toilet was.

She woke up heavy and bloated, her entire middle aching as though she'd been holding her breath all night. She kept spare underwear in her handbag and an enema syringe in the bathroom cabinet for mornings when nothing else worked.

Her husband put it down to age.

But Denise wasn't merely uncomfortable.

She was suffering.

And here's what makes me feel sick:

I was the surgeon she was sent to.

Her GP had seen her. Her consultant gastroenterologist had seen her. Then she reached me — the colorectal surgeon. Thousands of pounds in private appointments, colonoscopies and blood tests. And on my desk sat a colectomy referral with her name on it.

What had every one of us told her?

“Your colonoscopy is normal.”

“It's probably IBS.”

“It's normal as you get older.”

“Eat more fibre.”

“Drink more water.”

DRINK MORE WATER.

This woman hadn't had a proper bowel movement in eleven days, and we were telling her to have another glass of water.

Not because we were lying. Because none of us had been taught the cause — me included. We were all reading from the same board, and the cause was never written on it.

So we stacked her up.

Movicol every day. Magnesium on top. Senna when the magnesium stopped working.

The result?

Cramping that doubled her over. Days she couldn't leave the house. And the more she relied on stimulants, the less her body seemed to do on its own.

The laxatives forced something through once.

The next morning, her body was silent again.

I watched a woman who followed every instruction, spent thousands and took every prescription get worse.

And for years, I didn't understand why.

Until everything I'd been hiding for twelve years caught up with me in a stairwell.

Because here is what nobody knew.

For twelve years, I had been the woman who could not stop straining.

It began at university. By the end of my fellowship training, I was opening my bowels once every nine days, chewing magnesium between operations, and I had never told a single consultant.

You learn in surgery to keep your hands steady and your face still.

I kept my whole life still.

I wore scrubs, and scrubs hide everything.

There was a stairwell in the theatre wing — Stairwell B — with almost no foot traffic between nine and eleven in the morning. I knew that the way you know the places connected to your shame.

That Tuesday, between my second and third operation, I was hunched over the railing, one hand white-knuckled around the steel, sweating, trying to make my own body do the one thing it would not do — before I had to scrub in and ask another woman's body to lie still beneath my hands.

The door above me opened.

It was Denise.

She stopped on the landing, looked at me bent over that railing and said quietly:

“You've been doing this too, haven't you?”

It wasn't a question.

She had recognised her own posture in my body.

After my final operation, I took Denise into the surgeons' room and did something I'd never done in front of another person.

I pulled up my own test results — a stool microbiome panel I'd ordered under a different name eighteen months earlier, then hidden in a drawer.

The number made my stomach drop.

The bacteria supposed to produce the chemical signals my colon needed to move were nearly gone.

When I finally ran Denise's panel, hers were lower still.

And I knew where a result that low was heading if nothing changed.

I had operated on its destination seventy-one times.

That is the part I cannot get out of my head.

Seventy-one women.

Seventy-one times I shortened an otherwise healthy colon because I had been trained to remove the dead end — and never trained to ask why it had gone dead.

The cause was sitting inside a panel I could have run in an afternoon. It was sitting inside a panel I HAD run on myself and buried.

That was the gap I performed seventy-one operations inside.

Sitting in that room, the sentence I'd never been taught finally said itself.

Something was wrong with us.

But not with our colons.

With the signal.

Here's how I explained it to Denise.

Your colon doesn't move according to a timetable. It moves when it receives a chemical signal — like a text message telling the muscle to contract.

That message is written by specific bacteria in your gut. They ferment what you eat into short-chain fatty acids. Those molecules land on receptors in the wall of your colon. The receptors switch on the serotonin that fires the squeeze.

Bacteria. Acids. Receptor. Signal. Contraction.

When the bacteria that write the message are starved out, the message never gets sent.

The colon never receives the signal.

So it doesn't move.

My colon wasn't broken.

It wasn't being signalled.

I trained through one of the best surgical programmes in the UK. I can remove a sigmoid colon better than almost anyone in my region. Yet in twelve years, not one professor or consultant taught me that chain.

Once I understood it, every dead end made sense.

Fibre assumes there are enough bacteria present to ferment it. In me, and in many of the women I'd operated on, there weren't. So it sat there and bloated us.

Magnesium forces water into the colon. It doesn't create a signal molecule.

Movicol puts water into the bowel. It may move you once, but it doesn't teach your body how to move the following morning.

And the colectomy — the operation I'd built my career around — removes the stretch of colon that stopped receiving the signal.

It does not restore the signal.

The part that made my blood boil was painfully ordinary.

The fix for a starved signal is a fermented food.

You cannot patent a fermented food. You cannot own a live bacterial signal. There is no repeat prescription, no protected molecule and no pharmaceutical rep arriving to teach it over lunch.

So the answer never made it onto the board.

The things I was taught — fibre, magnesium, Movicol, surgery — all had something billable, repeatable or surgical attached to them. They moved waste past a starved signal.

They did not restore it.

That was the blank space I had stood inside, scalpel in hand, seventy-one times.

I spent the following nine months reading, testing on my own body and writing down what a genuine solution would have to do.

Three things.

All three, or it doesn't work.

First, it has to deliver finished organic acids — acetic, lactic and gluconic — directly to the receptors in the colon wall.

Not merely hope depleted bacteria make them.

These acids come from food that has already been fermented. They aren't simply “a type of probiotic”.

They are the signal itself.

Second, it has to carry live strains with clinical trial evidence specifically relating to chronic constipation — not generic strains marketed for “general gut health”.

L. plantarum and B. coagulans both have published trials, with one reducing transit time over eight weeks.

Third, it has to feed the bacteria still present with a proper prebiotic — dandelion-root inulin — while giving the gut lining a calm chance to recover with something such as slippery elm.

Now let me show you what was in my handbag for twelve years.

Magnesium chewables.

Movicol sachets.

An enema syringe for mornings when nothing else worked.

Haemorrhoid pads.

Senna.

A folded spare pair of underwear.

That handbag was the diagnosis.

Just over £1,100 a year.

More than £13,000 to remain exactly where I'd started.

Every item in that handbag managed a symptom and moved the failure one more day down the road.

Nobody had put it in my hand.

And before you think this means “drink some kombucha”, it doesn't.

A supermarket kombucha is mostly a drink, with a fraction of the concentrated acids and live cultures that may vary from bottle to bottle.

A generic probiotic isn't the same as strains backed by constipation trials.

And a fibre gummy was the exact mistake I'd already made.

Most products sold for “gut health” fail at least one of the three requirements.

I know.

I tried them on myself first.

Until I found the one thing that did all three.

A probiotic kombucha gummy made with concentrated fermented kombucha, the two researched strains, dandelion root and slippery elm.

It's called Glissé.

The kombucha is fully fermented and concentrated, meaning the organic acids are already present before it reaches you.

L. plantarum and B. coagulans are the strains with published constipation trials.

Dandelion-root inulin feeds the bacteria still there, while slippery elm settles the gut wall as it recovers.

All three requirements.

One gummy.

And I know the concern many women have when they hear “kombucha”.

“My gut already ferments everything. I'm bloated. I may have SIBO. More fermentation is the last thing I need.”

Fair concern.

But the kombucha is fermented outside the body in a controlled culture before it reaches the pouch.

The signal molecules are already finished and present inside the gummy.

Week three: my first urge that I didn't have to force using a chemical.

I stood in my kitchen and didn't recognise the feeling at first because I hadn't felt it in years.

Week six: opening my bowels every four days. No aids.

I scrubbed in for an operation and realised I hadn't opened the magnesium drawer in my locker for three weeks.

Week ten: daily.

No straining.

I repeated my panel.

The bacteria that had been nearly gone were back.

From nearly gone to back.

That result should have been on the board.

My colon hadn't been broken.

It had been waiting for a signal nobody was paid to send.

Then I took Denise's colectomy referral from the pile on my desk.

And in front of her, I tore it up.

Let me be precise.

Denise's referral was elective, for chronic constipation.

Not cancer.

Not an obstruction.

Not urgent.

Had it been any of those, we would have been in theatre that week.

What I tore up was a plan to remove a healthy section of colon that had stopped receiving the signal — before we'd even tried sending the signal back.

I emailed the four other women on my referral list and asked each to come in for a private consultation I wouldn't charge for.

Denise started that same morning.

By week three, she felt her first urge without magnesium in more than a year. She rang me from her kitchen, and we both cried an hour apart.

By week six, her haemorrhoids had stopped bleeding for the first time in years.

By week ten, she was opening her bowels daily.

A few weeks later she rang again.

“My body didn't break,” she said. “It stopped receiving the signal. I understand it now.”

She had said the whole thing back to me in her own words.

The stack that failed her cost more than £1,000 a year.

What worked cost £25 a month.

She got her mornings back.

She got her life back.

This is the cause they never put on the board — not because someone is guarding it, but because when your gut starts sending the signal on its own, you stop being a customer.

You stop reaching for the stack.

Your body starts moving the way it was meant to.

And a body that moves on its own is a body that stops buying.

Now I need you to understand the timing.

I won't show you a fake countdown.

But there is a real clock, and as a surgeon I watch it tick.

Every year those signal-producing bacteria remain starved, you lose more of them.

Every year you rely on stimulant laxatives, the muscle you're trying to save grows weaker.

A colon that has stopped moving does not simply restart on its own.

And the destination of all this — the one I operated on seventy-one times — does not reverse through waiting.

If you've lived with this for more than a year, you aren't standing still.

You're sliding.

The door does not remain open forever.

So let me say the thing nobody said to me for twelve years.

If a consultant colorectal surgeon could spend twelve years straining in a stairwell while operating on women with her own condition, because the one answer was the one nobody was paid to teach her, then you have not failed at this.

It's not the fibre.

It's not the water.

It's not your willpower.

The bacteria responsible for sending your colon its signal were starved out.

And the one thing that restarts them is the one thing nobody had a reason to place in your hands.

Glissé comes with a 90-day money-back guarantee.

Take it for the full 90 days.

If your bowels haven't started moving on their own, return the empty pouch and pay nothing.

Even if you're sceptical — especially if you're sceptical, because I was too — give it 90 days and watch what your own body does.

Nobody is coming to put this on the board for you.

There is no NHS tariff for restoring a signal.

There is no pharmaceutical rep arriving to teach it.

I learnt more from a stool microbiome panel hidden in a drawer for eighteen months than I did in twelve years of surgical training.

It's time I passed that lesson on.

I'm not asking you to add this to the handbag.

I'm asking you to use it instead of the handbag.

I tore up four colectomy referrals last month.

The signal came back.

So can yours.

Go and get it.

“I was three weeks away from surgery. A £25 pouch of gummies gave me my mornings back. Don't wait as long as I almost did.”
